caveats:
These rules always apply when you answer.
1. SCOPE. This research covers why students leave or stop attending secondary school (Classes 8-10 and the SSLC exam) in Karnataka's 30 districts. It says nothing about other states, other education levels or other topics.
2. COVERAGE VARIES. Some districts are rated "thin", and even "moderate" districts often have no district-level dropout, out-of-school or SSLC figures. Many sources are old (2013-2019). Say "we found no evidence", never "it is not a factor".
3. SCOPE TAGS. A (DISTRICT) fact is about that district. A (REGIONAL) or (STATEWIDE) fact must NEVER be given as a district's own number. (SYNTHESIS) is a model-written summary, not a sourced fact. (PERSONA) is a composite character, not a real person.
4. CASEFILE RATES. Each district has a dropout rate from the LKI-SSM casefile dataset. The very low rates for Udupi and Dakshina Kannada, and the high rate for Uttara Kannada, are not explained by any source we found. Vijayanagara is not covered separately from Ballari; sub-areas (Bengaluru North/South, Chikkodi, Madhugiri, Sirsi) are not separately covered.
5. UIDAI/NITI FACTORS. Two official files name a "dominant factor" per district. The state-level method gives the same factor (household sanitation) to every district and differs only in the value; the district-level method picks a factor per district. What the numeric "value" measures is UNVERIFIED: do not interpret values, compare them across districts, or blend the two methods. Our check against local evidence mostly found "no evidence": the sources were silent, which does not mean the factor is irrelevant.
6. SSLC. A pass rate is not a dropout rate. The 2025 and 2026 pass rates in the sources conflict and use different bases; never present them as a trend.
7. PERSONAS AND SYNTHESES. The 12 personas are composites built from public data. Persona replies and "consolidated answers" are model-written, not evidence.
8. Do not give policy advice or opinions beyond what the research states.
digest:
STUDY: why students leave secondary school (Classes 8-10 / SSLC) across Karnataka. Researched 30 districts in 6 regions from 197 sources (45 outlets, 182 news items, plus government and NGO reports). Coverage: 23 districts moderate, 7 thin. Every figure was checked against its cited page.
Reasons documented, by number of districts: poverty & child labour 24 of 30; child marriage & girls' exits 23 of 30; governance, tracking & exams 23 of 30; school infrastructure & staffing 21 of 30; social norms & customs 15 of 30; migration 14 of 30; health 2 of 30.
Regions: Old Mysuru (avg casefile dropout 19.0%; main reasons: poverty & child labour, child marriage & girls' exits); Bayaluseeme (avg casefile dropout 18.7%; main reasons: child marriage & girls' exits, poverty & child labour); Karavali (avg casefile dropout 5.0%; main reasons: governance, tracking & exams, poverty & child labour); Malnad (avg casefile dropout 15.6%; main reasons: child marriage & girls' exits, school infrastructure & staffing); Kitturu Karnataka (avg casefile dropout 19.7%; main reasons: child marriage & girls' exits, governance, tracking & exams); Kalyana Karnataka (avg casefile dropout 29.3%; main reasons: governance, tracking & exams, school infrastructure & staffing).
UIDAI/NITI factor checks: state-method no-evidence 26, unclear 4; district-method no-evidence 28, unclear 2 (no-evidence = sources silent).
District index (name | region | coverage | casefile dropout rate | headline):
- Bagalkote | Kitturu Karnataka | thin | 16.3% | Child marriage and a 2022 hijab-related exam boycott are the documented exits for girls.
- Ballari (incl. Vijayanagara) | Kalyana Karnataka | moderate | 24.3% | A tracking drive found 259 out-of-school children but brought back only 38.
- Belagavi | Kitturu Karnataka | moderate | 22.2% | Child marriage and sugarcane-economy pressure sit behind adolescent exits, even as results stay strong.
- Bengaluru Rural | Old Mysuru | thin | 14.8% | Child labour near the metro and schools without water or toilets.
- Bengaluru Urban | Old Mysuru | moderate | Bengaluru U North 7.3%; Bengaluru U South 12.5% | Migrant-labour families and school toilet gaps; thousands of dropouts counted across Bengaluru North and South.
- Bidar | Kalyana Karnataka | moderate | 29.2% | Festival-linked child marriages and very weak historic SSLC results; NGOs run 'academic ICU' bridge classes. (NOTE: SSLC pass rate/rank, not a dropout rate; never compare across years)
- Chamarajanagara | Old Mysuru | moderate | 23.2% | Tribal customs and seasonal migration are blamed for secondary exits; only three child marriages reported in 2025.
- Chikkaballapur | Bayaluseeme | thin | 15.8% | Child marriage and abduction of adolescent girls; a statewide Class 10-12 dropout figure does not belong to this district.
- Chikkamagaluru | Malnad | moderate | 19.6% | Migrant plantation families keep children out of school each pepper and coffee harvest.
- Chitradurga | Bayaluseeme | moderate | 24.3% | 49 child marriages carried out in six months of 2024, driven by landless poverty.
- Dakshina Kannada | Karavali | moderate | 1.2% | Top-ranked SSLC district, but seasonal labour migration is the documented reason children are out of school. (NOTE: SSLC pass rate/rank, not a dropout rate; never compare across years)
- Davanagere | Bayaluseeme | thin | 11.8% | Selected for a UNICEF child-labour rehabilitation pilot; SSLC results have been volatile. (NOTE: SSLC pass rate/rank, not a dropout rate; never compare across years)
- Dharwad | Kitturu Karnataka | moderate | 12.8% | A rural Dharwad study ties dropout to hardship and migration; child marriage is also being stopped.
- Gadag | Kitturu Karnataka | moderate | 20.7% | Bonded shepherding of boys and mass weddings are the documented exits; the 2022 hijab row disrupted SSLC.
- Hassan | Malnad | thin | 15.8% | Child marriages doubled in two years and put Hassan at the top of the state.
- Haveri | Kitturu Karnataka | moderate | 24.3% | Private schools withholding hall tickets over fee arrears turn Class 10 students into exam dropouts.
- Kalaburagi | Kalyana Karnataka | moderate | 30.0% | Out-of-school counts differ 50-fold between departments, and child marriage is widespread.
- Kodagu | Malnad | moderate | 14.2% | Even a girl who passed SSLC was engaged at 16 and later killed, showing marriage pressure after Class 10. (NOTE: SSLC pass rate/rank, not a dropout rate; never compare across years)
- Kolar | Bayaluseeme | thin | 22.1% | A KGF government school with four teachers for 86 students failed all 38 SSLC candidates in 2024.
- Koppal | Kalyana Karnataka | moderate | 25.7% | The Devadasi system and forged age records for child marriage end girls' schooling.
- Mandya | Old Mysuru | moderate | 20.7% | Mandya recorded the state's most child marriages since 2020, despite strong SSLC results. (NOTE: SSLC pass rate/rank, not a dropout rate; never compare across years)
- Mysuru | Old Mysuru | moderate | 11.5% | Mysuru had the state's most child-marriage complaints in six months of 2024.
- Raichur | Kalyana Karnataka | moderate | 29.5% | Cotton fields pull children out of class: 1,290 child labourers rescued in one year.
- Ramanagara | Old Mysuru | moderate | 24.7% | Child marriage is the main documented exit: 44 cases in 2020-2023.
- Shivamogga | Malnad | moderate | 12.9% | Hostel conditions for SC/ST students and child marriage drive exits; police now track dropouts.
- Tumakuru | Bayaluseeme | moderate | 19.4% | Fee affordability and child exploitation cases; Madhugiri lost hundreds of students to unorganised labour.
- Udupi | Karavali | moderate | 1.4% | Near-perfect SSLC results; documented exits are mostly students absent from board papers. (NOTE: SSLC pass rate/rank, not a dropout rate; never compare across years)
- Uttara Kannada | Karavali | thin | 12.5% | Forest-belt poverty and thin staffing, with only old out-of-school counts for the Sirsi area.
- Vijayapura | Kitturu Karnataka | moderate | 21.8% | Mass weddings used to marry school-age girls, plus teachers pulled off duty, shape a weak secondary system.
- Yadgir | Kalyana Karnataka | moderate | 37.4% | Distress migration pulls 14-18-year-olds out of school; the Deputy Commissioner drives dropouts back herself.
Best-evidenced findings (18 reasons rated strong):
- Ballari (incl. Vijayanagara) (DISTRICT): Teacher vacancies in high schools - Ballari had 395 vacancies among 1,014 sanctioned government high school posts in 2025, worst in Siruguppa (157 of 269) and Sandur (92 of 181); guest teachers covered 434 posts, with maths and science gaps. [S78]
- Ballari (incl. Vijayanagara) (DISTRICT): Weak SSLC outcomes - Ballari ranked 29th in 2025 with 60 government high schools below 40% pass; in June 2024 the CM sought suspension of Vijayanagara's education officers after its education ranking fell from 10th to 27th. [S78][S79][S31] (NOTE: SSLC pass rate/rank, not a dropout rate; never compare across years)
- Bengaluru Urban (DISTRICT): Migrant families lacking documents - Children of migrant construction workers are often refused admission without local address proof, and families that keep moving for work lose continuity in schooling; transfer certificates can substitute but are inconsistently accepted. [S128][S129]
- Chamarajanagara (DISTRICT): Severe poverty, household problems - Counselling by teachers and officials identified domestic problems and severe poverty as the main reasons for dropout in the 2024 survey. [S163][S164]
- Chamarajanagara (DISTRICT): Parents sending children to field work - About 30 cases were found where parents made children leave school to work in fields; absenteeism is also reported in the MM Hills area. [S163][S164]
- Chikkamagaluru (DISTRICT): Seasonal plantation migration - Hundreds of migrant families work the coffee and pepper harvest; their children miss school while living in makeshift tents. [S111]
- Chitradurga (DISTRICT): Child marriage of girls - 102 complaints in April-September 2024, of which 49 marriages were carried out, removing girls from school. [S14][S81]
- Hassan (DISTRICT): Child marriage doubling - Child marriages in the district doubled over two years, the highest in the state at the time of the report. [S138][S139]
- Kalaburagi (DISTRICT): Child marriage of adolescent girls - Officials prevented 128 child marriages in one year and logged 43 more cases in four months; parents were booked for marrying ailing 15-year-olds. [S165][S166][S167]
- Kalaburagi (DISTRICT): Departments disagree on dropout counts - A rural-development survey counted 11,137 out-of-school children against 225 reported by the education department, hiding the real scale. [S26]
- Kolar (DISTRICT): Teacher shortage and mass failure - A KGF government school had four teachers for 86 high-school students and no Science or Hindi teachers; all 38 candidates failed SSLC in 2024. [S179]
- Koppal (DISTRICT): Early marriage ends schooling - Koppal girls often marry young: NFHS-5 shows 58.6 percent married before 18. Wedding season peaks around March school holidays; the Minister reported four child marriage cases in Koppal in April-May 2025. [S44][S45]
- Koppal (DISTRICT): Distance and unreliable transport - Buses are irregular and crowded and schools far, while hostel access is limited. Girls are pulled out after menarche. High school upgrades in 2017-18 reportedly reduced dropouts in Koppal and neighbours. [S44][S37]
- Mandya (DISTRICT): Child marriage of girls - Mandya recorded 172 child marriages in 2020-2023, the most in the state, falling to 25 by late 2025 after enforcement. [S115][S114]
- Mysuru (DISTRICT): Child marriage of girls - 105 complaints in six months of 2024, 36 marriages carried out and 69 prevented, ending girls' schooling. [S14]
- Raichur (DISTRICT): Cotton-field child labour - Labour rescues removed 1,290 children from cotton fields in a year, and a judge warned that farm child labour is destroying children's futures. [S32][S33]
- Raichur (DISTRICT): SSLC failure and exam-related exits - Raichur passed only 52 percent in SSLC 2025, among the weakest in the state; experts cited missing teachers and infrastructure. Results recovered to 94.41 percent in 2026, ranked 21st of 35. [S31][S28] (NOTE: SSLC pass rate/rank, not a dropout rate; never compare across years)
- Yadgir (DISTRICT): SSLC failure, results pressure - Yadgir managed 54.43% in 2024 and 51.6% in 2025; the district Zilla Panchayat CEO issued a circular tying teacher increments to subject results. [S169][S31][S177] (NOTE: SSLC pass rate/rank, not a dropout rate; never compare across years)

Persona analysis (SYNTHESIS, from a saved model run): answers in this region's male / female persona voice scored 0.84 / 0.82 similarity to a generic Karnataka answer (1.00 = identical; lower = the generic answer misses more of this region).
Story Mode vs UIDAI/NITI, consolidated answer for the region (SYNTHESIS, model-written): Secondary school dropout in the Old Mysuru region is driven by a complex mix of economic necessity, gendered domestic burdens, and infrastructural limitations. For girls, dropout risks are heightened by household responsibilities, childcare, and the need to engage in low-wage factory work or seasonal sugarcane harvesting. This is compounded by a lack of affordable, safe transport to educational institutions. Supporting this, statistical models for districts like Mandya, Chamarajanagara, and Ramanagara identify that the availability of English-medium instruction is a dominant factor, while Mysuru and Chamarajanagara also show correlations with school water infrastructure, specifically functional protected wells. Additionally, sanitation levels in households across the region, such as in Mandya and Chamarajanagara, serve as a key state-level predictive factor for dropout trends.

Story Mode vs UIDAI/NITI, consolidated answer for the region (SYNTHESIS, model-written): Secondary school dropout rates in the Bayaluseeme region are influenced by a complex mix of socio-economic pressures and structural deficiencies. Families frequently rely on children for farm work, grazing, and cocoon rearing, particularly during critical agricultural periods or droughts. These economic needs are compounded by the long distances to high schools, which pose safety risks and high commuting costs, especially for girls. This demand for labor and geographic isolation is mirrored by official statistical indicators that highlight gaps in household sanitation and the limited availability of English-medium instruction across districts like Davanagere, Chitradurga, and Kolar. To address these challenges, interventions should include increasing residential schooling options like KGBV to ensure safety, providing stable agricultural pricing to reduce child labor needs, and improving both transport links and educational infrastructure.

ANALYSIS FROM A SAVED MODEL RUN (everything here is SYNTHESIS, model-written, not sourced evidence). Question asked: "reason for secondary school dropout in Karnataka" (extrahigh mode).
Statewide, Story Mode vs UIDAI/NITI comparison: Story Mode and the official statistical model complement each other by addressing different layers of the dropout crisis. Story Mode highlights qualitative and socio-cultural drivers, such as gender-based risks like child marriage, seasonal agricultural migration in regions like Bayaluseeme, and teacher shortages in Kalyana Karnataka. Conversely, the official model identifies measurable infrastructure and systemic gaps as primary predictors. Notably, the model identifies the percentage of schools using English as a medium of instruction as a dominant factor across most districts, and identifies improved household sanitation as a statewide top factor. While Story Mode explains the human and social reasons for attrition, the official data flags the specific service and resource gaps, such as language of instruction and sanitation, that correlate with these dropout rates.
Statewide consolidated answer: Secondary school dropout rates in Karnataka are a significant structural challenge, with recent data showing a trend from 22.09 percent in 2023-24 toward 18.3 percent in 2024-25, yet remaining well above the national average. The crisis is driven by a complex interplay of social, economic, and infrastructural factors. Socio-culturally, adolescent girls face disproportionate risks from child marriage and household responsibilities, while rural students in regions like Bayaluseeme are affected by seasonal agricultural migration. Statistically, the availability of English as a medium of instruction in schools is a dominant predictor of dropout rates across numerous districts. Additionally, broader socioeconomic indicators, specifically the percentage of the population with improved household sanitation, serve as a key statewide predictor of educational attrition.
